raw_response:
**My reasoning:**

My family has farmed this land in Quzhou for generations. The North China Plain is wheat and maize country — that's what the soil knows, that's what the buyers want, and that's what I know how to grow. I have about 8 mu of flat, irrigated cropland. I will do what my father did and what my neighbors do: plant winter wheat in October after the summer harvest, then follow it with summer maize. Same fields, same rotation, same rhythm.

I know the well is running lower every year, but I still irrigate three times for wheat — you skip the jointing water and you lose the grain. For maize I can usually get by with less if the rains come in July. I buy hybrid maize seed from the village cooperative because the yields are noticeably better than saving my own. For wheat I use the improved variety the township promoted a few years ago — it has decent resistance to rust.

For fertilizer I spread compound fertilizer as a base before planting and top-dress with urea at the right growth stage. I go by feel and by what the other men around me do — I don't have a soil test. I probably put on a bit more nitrogen than needed but I'd rather not risk a thin crop. Two pesticide passes on each crop — one early for insects, one around heading/tasseling for disease.
